title: A Dead Star Is Flashing Radio Waves Every 8 Minutes - Nautilus
gist: Astronomers report in Nature Astronomy the first long-period radio transient traced to a white dwarf orbiting a Sun-like G-type star, pulsing every 7.9 minutes in a 32-hour orbit; it suggests radio surveys could reveal a hidden population of white-dwarf binaries relevant to Type Ia supernova cosmology.

themes.theme: New source for long-period radio transients

insights.claim: Long-period radio transients, a class of object discovered in 2022 that flashes radio waves every few minutes to hours, had previously been traced mostly to binaries of a white dwarf and a small red dwarf.
insights.so_what: Establishes the baseline the new discovery breaks.
insights.quote: a pattern has emerged: a binary system of a white dwarf and a small, cool red dwarf
insights.speaker: Natasha Hurley-Walker

insights.claim: Slow-spinning neutron star pulsars were ruled out as the explanation for long-period radio transients because, in theory, a neutron star spinning that slowly should not produce radio waves.
insights.so_what: Shows the theoretical constraints driving the white-dwarf interpretation.
insights.speaker: Natasha Hurley-Walker

insights.claim: In late 2024 the Murchison Widefield Array, using a search method developed by PhD student Csanád Horváth, detected radio flashes every 7.9 minutes that appear only in a ~6-hour window followed by 26 hours of silence, implying a binary with a 32-hour orbit.
insights.so_what: Novel search algorithms on existing arrays are finding new object classes.
insights.quote: The pulses only appear during a window of about six hours, followed by 26 hours without pulses.
insights.speaker: Natasha Hurley-Walker

insights.claim: MeerKAT pinpointed the source and Keck spectroscopy showed the companion is a G-type star almost the same mass and temperature as the Sun, not a red dwarf.
insights.so_what: First white dwarf pulsar found orbiting a Sun-like star.
insights.quote: this was not a tiny red dwarf, but a G-type star almost the same mass and temperature as our own Sun
insights.locator: The MeerKAT telescope in South Africa
insights.speaker: Natasha Hurley-Walker

insights.claim: Pulse-timing shifts of up to four seconds and the Sun-like star's minimal wobble imply the pulsing object weighs about two-thirds of a solar mass, too light to be a neutron star, so the authors conclude it is a white dwarf pulsar.
insights.so_what: Methodology combining radio timing and optical spectra to weigh unseen objects.
insights.quote: the pulsing object is about two-thirds as heavy as the Sun. That means it’s too light to be a neutron star
insights.speaker: Natasha Hurley-Walker

insights.claim: The authors propose the system formed when the white dwarf's progenitor swelled into a giant, engulfed its companion, and shrank the orbit before ejecting its outer layers.
insights.speaker: Natasha Hurley-Walker

insights.claim: Such white dwarf–bright star systems are probably common but hidden by the bright star's glare, and radio pulses could let surveys uncover a population that optical and X-ray telescopes miss.
insights.so_what: Supports the scientific case for radio-astronomy investment over optical/X-ray for this niche.
insights.quote: radio surveys could uncover a whole undiscovered population that optical and X-ray telescopes miss
insights.speaker: Natasha Hurley-Walker

insights.claim: Because some white dwarf binaries are thought to be ancestors of Type Ia supernovae used as 'standard candles' to measure cosmic distances and expansion, finding more of them could refine that process.
insights.speaker: Natasha Hurley-Walker

insights.claim: The authors expect next-generation radio telescopes such as the SKA Observatory to find many more of these systems.
insights.so_what: SKA build-out is a demand driver for radio-astronomy hardware and computing.
insights.quote: With the next generation of radio telescopes, such as the SKA Observatory, we expect to find many more.
insights.speaker: Natasha Hurley-Walker
